passage: You brought that tiffin and didn't say a word, Hansa. I remember the steel lid clinking on my table. I'm Santosh, the one who always has a joke, and after Baba died I had none. Every relative who came had a sentence ready. You just sat. I ate half a roti and you didn't comment. That silence was the kindest thing anyone gave me that week. But by the third week the house had gone quiet, people had gone back to their lives, and I felt the drop. So I told you plainly: "Could you come for a walk on Sundays, and could you say his name sometimes?" You said yes, and you did. I'd never have guessed that asking would be the hard part, but it changed everything.

qa.q: What did Hansa bring to Santosh's house?
Why did Hansa's silence feel kind to Santosh?
qa.a: Grieving Baba and without words, Santosh felt comforted by Hansa's steady presence instead of the ready sentences relatives offered.

qa.q: What did Santosh ask for in the weeks after, and why then?
qa.a: A Sunday walk and to hear Baba's name sometimes, because by the third week the house went quiet and support had faded.

qa.q: How might Hansa have seen Santosh's request?
qa.a: Probably as welcome and clear, since Hansa said yes and kept doing it. Knowing what to do can be easier than guessing. 🤍

grounding: Friends bring food and sit silently; the grieving person accepts and, since support fades, says what is needed in the weeks after.

passage:
"Francis, you asked how I got through the year your grandmother died. I was twenty-six. Let me tell you.

For the first week, I, Abhinav, couldn't speak. People came to the flat with food: dal, rice, even a whole cake from the bakery downstairs. My friend Joseph came every evening and just sat. He didn't say anything clever. He washed the dishes, sat beside me on the sofa, and left at ten.

I felt guilty that I couldn't even thank them. But I let them come.

After a month, everyone went back to their lives. The house went quiet, and that was the hardest part. So I did something I'd never done. I called Joseph and said, 'Can you keep coming on Sundays? Just Sundays.' He did, for a whole year.

Wise words didn't save me, boy. Dal and a friend on the sofa did."

qa.q: What did Joseph do on his evening visits?
qa.a: He washed the dishes, sat on the sofa beside Abhinav and left at ten.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel about not being able to thank the visitors?
qa.a: Abhinav felt guilty for not speaking or thanking them, but accepted their help anyway.

qa.q: What choice did Abhinav make when support faded after a month, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Abhinav asked Joseph to keep coming on Sundays, telling a friend exactly what was needed once the house went quiet.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen his quiet visits?
qa.a: Joseph seems to have understood that his steady presence mattered more than words, so he kept coming for a year.

grounding: An elder recalls friends bringing food and sitting silently after a death, accepting the help without speaking, and asking a friend for continued support when it faded.

passage:
The rain hadn't stopped in Guwahati for three days, and the power in Nazia's lane had been out since the morning of her father's burial. The streets were knee-deep. Most relatives had gone home before the water rose.

That evening, someone knocked. Kishore, from her office, stood soaked to the thighs, holding a steel tiffin above his head. "Biryani," he said. "My mother made it. I couldn't find a rickshaw."

Nazia couldn't speak. She just stepped aside.

He didn't say anything wise. He lit a candle, sat on the floor across from her, and they ate from the tiffin. When she started crying, he passed her a napkin and kept sitting.

At the door, he said, "I'll come back. What do you need?"

She thought. "In a month, when everyone's forgotten. Come then. Remind me to eat."

"The fifteenth," Kishore said. "I'll write it down."

qa.q: What did Kishore bring in the tiffin?
What was Nazia feeling when she couldn't speak at the door?
qa.a: She felt grief-stricken and deeply moved that Kishore had waded through the flood to bring food.

qa.q: What did Nazia do that will help in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: She told Kishore exactly what she needed later, a visit in a month to remind her to eat, knowing support fades.

qa.q: How does Kishore see his role that evening?
qa.a: Kishore sees it as simply being there, sitting and sharing food without needing wise words.

grounding: Under the constraint of floods and a power cut, the passage shows a grieving young woman accepting a friend's food and silent company, and telling him what she will need in the weeks after.
